This repository already contains `accounts`, a command-line tool that manages local user accounts with passwords in a single store file. Read the existing code and any documentation in the repository before changing it. Add password reset as described below; every existing command must keep working exactly as it does now.

- `python -m accounts --store PATH reset-token USERNAME [--ttl SECONDS]` creates a one-time password-reset token for the account and prints it on a line of its own to standard output; an administrator passes it on to the user. The token is valid for SECONDS seconds, 900 (15 minutes) by default.
- `python -m accounts --store PATH reset USERNAME` reads the token and then the new password from standard input, one per line. If the token is valid, it sets the new password and prints `password reset`. A token can be used only once. A wrong, already used or expired token prints `invalid token` to standard error and exits with status 1. A new password shorter than 12 characters is rejected with exit status 2, and the token can still be used afterwards.
- For both commands, a username that does not exist fails with exit status 3.

Successful commands exit with status 0.

Examples, with a store `users.db`:

```
$ printf 'correct horse battery\n' | python -m accounts --store users.db register alice
registered alice
$ python -m accounts --store users.db reset-token alice
(a token on one line, for example 3Hk2...)
$ printf 'not-the-token\nbrand new password\n' | python -m accounts --store users.db reset alice
invalid token        <- on standard error; exit status 1
$ python -m accounts --store users.db reset-token nobody
(an error message on standard error; exit status 3)
```

Done — password reset is implemented, tested, and documented. All 90 tests pass (the 59 pre-existing ones unchanged).

## What I added

**`src/accounts/tokens.py`** (new) — token generation, hashing and expiry:
- Token is `secrets.token_urlsafe(32)` (256 bits), printed once by `reset-token`.
- The store keeps only a SHA-256 digest plus `issued_at`/`expires_at`, so a stolen store file yields no usable tokens. A plain digest suffices here (unlike passwords): a 256-bit random token can't be guessed or dictionary-attacked.
- An entry whose expiry can't be parsed counts as expired.

**`src/accounts/service.py:reset_token` / `reset`** — issue and consume tokens. `reset` verifies the token first, then the password length; a short password writes nothing to the store, so the token survives. A successful reset deletes the token entry (that's what makes it one-time) and rehashes with a fresh salt.

**`src/accounts/cli.py`** — `reset-token` and `reset` added to the existing flat parser, plus `--ttl SECONDS` (positive integer, default 900). I kept the flat parser rather than switching to subparsers so every existing invocation form, including `--store` after the command, behaves byte-for-byte as before; `--ttl` with any other command is a usage error (status 2).

**`errors.py`** — `InvalidTokenError`, message `invalid token`, status 1.

Exit statuses match the spec: 0 success, 1 wrong/used/expired token, 2 short password (token still usable), 3 unknown user for both commands.

## Judgment calls (all recorded in the README)

- A successful `reset` also clears the lock and failed-attempt counter — otherwise a locked-out user resets their password and still can't log in. `reset-token`/`reset` work on a locked account for the same reason, and failed resets don't feed the lockout counter.
- Issuing a token invalidates any earlier one.
- The token line is stripped of surrounding whitespace (a token never contains whitespace, so this only forgives copy-paste and can't make an invalid token valid); passwords are still taken verbatim.
- `reset-token`/`reset` report unknown users as `no such user` (status 3) as specified, even though `login` deliberately doesn't disclose that.
- Bumped `__version__` to 1.1.0.
